definition.text: Putting an economic value on the environment and natural resources, many of which have no market price.

facts.text: Without dollar values for benefits such as clean air and water, estimates of pollution-control benefits fall below true social benefits and policy chronically underinvests.
Valuation is controversial: some environmentalists object to pricing what may be priceless, though such values keep society from ignoring nature in policy choices.
Willingness to pay is budget constrained and tends to be lower where incomes are lower, raising equity problems; willingness to accept is not and can in theory approach infinity.

title: Direct damage-cost valuation

definition.text: Valuing environmental improvement as the reduction in the monetary damage costs of pollution.

facts.text: Types include production damage (air pollution lowering corn yields), avoided cost (green roofs avoiding storm sewer spending) and health cost measures.

The Cabezas text calls these measures deeply problematic: they often give woefully incomplete estimates, since a cancer victim's medical bills are far below what her family would pay to avoid the illness.
